---
title: "Building a forecast"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
requireNamespace("xts", quietly = TRUE)
```

A series' *history* ends at its last observation. Forecasting it means
filling in the values from there to the end of the bank, from assumptions
about how it will grow or where it will be at certain dates. fcutils calls
this *extending* the series.

This article takes the Hawaii payroll jobs in `quarterly_data_example`,
whose history ends in 2025Q1, and extends them to 2035 with `extend()`,
`addf()`, `disagg()` and `chain()`, then averages the result to
years with `agg()`. The assumptions are made up for the example. If the
bank or the series names are new to you, read
[Getting started](getting-started.html) first.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(fcutils)
options(
  fcutils.bnk_start = as.Date("1998-01-01"),
  fcutils.bnk_end = as.Date("2035-12-31")
)
q <- conv_xts(quarterly_data_example)
jobs <- q$E_NF_HI
```

Every series that `extend()` and `addf()` return runs from the bank start to
the bank end, so results line up with each other and with the bank. Before
the last observation they hold the history; after it, the forecast.

## Which function

Each step below continues a series from something we know or assume about
its future. The form of that knowledge picks the function:

| What we know about the future | Function |
|---|---|
| Levels at some dates | `extend(type = "level")` |
| Growth rates at some dates, or a growth path, annualized or year over year | `extend(type = "growth", growth = "pca" or "pcy")` |
| Another series' path, such as a projection, for one series | `extend(type = "chain", method = "ratio" or "diff")` |
| Two sources of the same data to join, many series at once, or a series to extend back in time | `chain()` |

`extend()` forecasts one series and returns it on the bank. `chain()` joins
data and keeps the span of its inputs. Both use "ratio" to continue with
growth (levels) and "diff" to continue with changes in points (rates).

## Growth through anchors

An *anchor* is a target value at a date. With `type = "growth"`, the
anchors are growth rates, and they are *annualized*: the growth over one
quarter, compounded over four quarters, so that 1.2 means a pace of 1.2% a
year. `extend()` draws a straight line between the last observed growth
rate and the first anchor, and between each anchor and the next. It holds
the last anchor to the end of the bank. The level then grows from the last
observation at those rates.

Total jobs grew at an annualized `r round(as.numeric(pcmp(jobs, 1, 4)["2025-01-01"]), 1)`%
in 2025Q1. Here growth slows to 1.2% by 2025Q4 and to 0.8% by 2027Q4:

```{r}
jobs_fc <- extend(jobs, 2025.4 ~ 1.2, 2027.4 ~ 0.8, type = "growth")
round(pcmp(jobs_fc, lag = 1, comp_freq = 4)[p(2025.1, 2028.1)], 2)
```

Each anchor is a formula with the date on the left and the value on the
right. A decimal date is a quarter, so `2025.4` is 2025Q4. The same anchors
can be written with quoted dates, as a named vector, or with `at` and
`val`; all four calls give the same series:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
extend(jobs, "2025Q4" ~ 1.2, "2027Q4" ~ 0.8, type = "growth")
extend(jobs, val = c("2025Q4" = 1.2, "2027Q4" = 0.8), type = "growth")
extend(jobs, at = c(2025.4, 2027.4), val = c(1.2, 0.8), type = "growth")
```

A monthly series needs quoted months (`"2026M10" ~ 1.2`), because R reads
`2026.10` as `2026.1`. Anchors dated at or before the last observation are
dropped, with a message naming them: history takes precedence.

Growth is often quoted year over year instead, as for CPI inflation. With
`growth = "pcy"`, the anchors are year-over-year rates and each quarter
grows from the same quarter a year earlier:

```{r}
jobs_yy <- extend(jobs, 2025.4 ~ 1.2, 2027.4 ~ 0.8, type = "growth", growth = "pcy")
round(tsbox::ts_pcy(jobs_yy)[p(2025.1, 2028.1)], 2)
```

Year-over-year growth carries last year's quarter-to-quarter pattern into
the forecast: a quarter that was weak a year ago stays weak relative to its
neighbours. Annualized growth gives a smooth path from the last quarter.

## A level through anchors

With the default `type = "level"`, the series itself runs through the
anchors. Construction's share of jobs is `r round(100 * as.numeric(q$ECT_HI["2025-01-01"] / jobs["2025-01-01"]), 2)`%
in 2025Q1. Here it rises to 6.4% by 2026Q4 and eases to 6.0% by 2029Q4.
`interp = "stine"` (the Stineman spline) turns smoothly through the anchors
without overshooting them; the default, `"linear"`, draws straight lines.

```{r, fig.alt = "Construction share of jobs, 2022 to 2031: history, then the linear path with corners at the anchors and the smooth Stineman spline through the same anchors."}
share <- 100 * q$ECT_HI / jobs
paths <- tsbox::ts_c(
  linear = extend(share, 2026.4 ~ 6.4, 2029.4 ~ 6.0),
  stine = extend(share, 2026.4 ~ 6.4, 2029.4 ~ 6.0, interp = "stine")
)
tsbox::ts_plot(paths[p(2022, 2031)], title = "Construction share of jobs, %")
```

## Add-factors from ramps

An add-factor is a series added to a forecast to shift it for a while.
`addf()` builds one from a table of *ramps*: each row is a straight line
from `from` at `start` to `to` at `end`, and the add-factor is zero outside
the ramps. Overlapping ramps add up. Here a project raises the
construction share by up to 0.3 points over 2026–2029:

```{r}
ramps <- tibble::tribble(
  ~start, ~end,   ~from, ~to,
  2026.1, 2027.4, 0,     0.3,
  2028.1, 2029.4, 0.3,   0
)
adj <- addf(ramps, per = "quarter")
```

`adj` is a quarterly series over the whole bank. Adding it to the smooth
path from the previous section gives the adjusted share. Side by side:

```{r}
share_fc <- paths$stine + adj
round(tsbox::ts_c(share = paths$stine, adj = adj, adjusted = share_fc)[p(2025.4, 2030.1)], 3)
```

The first ramp climbs from 0 in 2026Q1 to 0.3 in 2027Q4, by 0.3 / 7 =
0.043 points a quarter. The second starts at 0.3 in 2028Q1 and falls back
to 0 by 2029Q4, so the adjusted share meets the 6.0 anchor there. Before
2026Q1 and after 2029Q4, `adj` is zero.

The dates can also be strings (`"2026Q1"`), and the same add-factor can be
written as points joined by straight lines:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ramps <- tibble::tribble(
  ~start,   ~end,     ~from, ~to,
  "2026Q1", "2027Q4", 0,     0.3,
  "2028Q1", "2029Q4", 0.3,   0
)
addf(2026.1 ~ 0, 2027.4 ~ 0.3, 2028.1 ~ 0.3, 2029.4 ~ 0)
```

Points also take `interp = "stine"`, which joins them with a smooth curve
that eases off zero and back, like the spline in `extend()`:

```{r, fig.alt = "Add-factor from 2025 to 2030: straight ramps up to 0.3 and back down, and a smooth curve through the same points that leaves and returns to zero gradually."}
adj_paths <- tsbox::ts_c(
  linear = adj,
  stine = addf(2026.1 ~ 0, 2027.4 ~ 0.3, 2028.1 ~ 0.3, 2029.4 ~ 0, interp = "stine")
)
tsbox::ts_plot(adj_paths[p(2025, 2030.4)], title = "Add-factor, points")
```

Construction jobs follow from the adjusted share and the total. Because
the share and the total both span the bank, ordinary arithmetic lines them
up:

```{r}
ct_fc <- share_fc / 100 * jobs_fc
round(ct_fc[p(2025.1, 2026.4)], 2)
```

## Following a projection

Sometimes the forecast for a series comes from elsewhere, such as a
projection by another agency. Its level may not match UHERO's history, for
example because it uses a different definition. With `type = "chain"`,
`extend()` takes only the growth of the projection, `path`, and applies it
to the series from its last observation. Suppose an annual projection of
government jobs for 2025–2035:

```{r}
gv_a <- make_xts(2025, val = seq(131, by = 0.8, length.out = 11))
```

The history is quarterly, so the projection must be quarterly too.
`disagg()` interpolates it to quarters whose averages equal the annual
values. Without anything to follow at the end of the series, the
interpolation bends toward zero growth over the last year;
`extend_with = "last_growth"` prevents that by continuing the series at its
last growth rate before interpolating.

```{r}
gv_q <- disagg(gv_a, extend_with = "last_growth")
round(tsbox::ts_c(annual = gv_a, quarterly_avg = agg(gv_q))[p(2025, 2027)], 3)
```

`extend()` then continues the quarterly history with the growth of the
interpolated projection:

```{r}
gv_fc <- extend(q$EGV_HI, path = gv_q, type = "chain")
gv <- tsbox::ts_c(history = q$EGV_HI, projection = gv_q, forecast = gv_fc)
round(gv[p(2024.4, 2025.4)], 2)
```

In 2025Q1 the projection is
`r round(as.numeric(gv_q["2025-01-01"] - q$EGV_HI["2025-01-01"]), 1)`
thousand above history. The forecast starts from history and grows from
quarter to quarter at the projection's rate, so the gap stays the same in
percent:

```{r}
round(pcmp(gv[, c("projection", "forecast")], lag = 1)[p(2025.2, 2025.4)], 3)
```

`method = "diff"` instead moves the projection by a constant to meet the
history, so the forecast keeps the projection's changes rather than its
growth rates. It suits rates, and levels whose gap to the projection should
stay constant in units rather than in percent.

## Updating a forecast bank

`chain()` does the same for many series at once. A common use is
updating a forecast when new data arrive. Suppose last time's forecast was
built on history to 2023Q4, and the data now run to 2025Q1. Rather than set
every assumption again, keep the growth that the old forecast had for each
series, and apply it from the new last observation.

The old forecast here is made up: each of the 30 series extended from
2023Q4 at 1% annualized growth. `extend()` works on one series at a time.
To apply it to all of them, stack the series in a long table, extend each
group, and turn the result back into xts:

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(dplyr)

old_hist <- q[p("", 2023.4)]
old_fc <- old_hist |>
  conv_long() |>
  group_by(id) |>
  group_modify(\(series, key) extend(series, 2024.1 ~ 1, type = "growth")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  conv_xts()
```

`chain()` then pairs each series in the new history `q` with the series of
the same name in `old_fc`:

```{r}
new_fc <- chain(q, old_fc, direction = "forward", verbose = FALSE)
compare <- tsbox::ts_c(old = old_fc$E_NF_HI, new = new_fc$E_NF_HI)
round(compare[p(2023.3, 2025.3)], 2)
```

For total jobs, the two agree to 2023Q4, where the old history ended. From
2024Q1 to 2025Q1 the new forecast is the new history, and after that it
grows at the old forecast's 1%, starting from the new 2025Q1 level of
`r round(as.numeric(q$E_NF_HI["2025-01-01"]), 1)` rather than the
`r round(as.numeric(old_fc$E_NF_HI["2025-01-01"]), 1)` the old forecast
had reached. The other 29 series are updated the same way.

If the names differ in their endings, such as `UR_AT_US_Q` (quarterly
history) and `UR_AT_US_SOLQ` (quarterly model output), `match = "stem"` pairs them on
the part before the ending. For rates such as the unemployment rate,
`method = "diff"` continues with the change in points instead of the growth
rate. A bank that mixes levels and rates takes one method per series, by
name: `method = c(UR_AT_US = "diff", FFR_AT_US = "diff")`, with "ratio" for
the rest. `direction = "backward"` extends a short history back in time with
the growth of a longer series.

## Annual results

Forecasts are usually reported as annual figures. `agg()` averages the
quarters of each complete year. Only complete years count, so a year with
three quarters of data has no value. Jobs are a count at a point in time,
so the average is right. For flows, such as visitor arrivals, the annual
figure is the total, so use `conv_type = "sum"`:

```{r}
fc <- tsbox::ts_c(E_NF_HI = jobs_fc, ECT_HI = ct_fc, EGV_HI = gv_fc)
round(agg(fc)[p(2024, 2028)], 1)
```

When an annual history differs from the average of its quarters (because
it averages unadjusted months, say), `chain(annual_history,
agg(fc), direction = "forward")` keeps the annual history and continues it
with the growth of the annual averages of the forecast.

[Growth rates, tables and plots](growth-and-reporting.html) shows how to
look at the result.
